title: What a file is, what a folder is

claims.text: The hierarchical file system was described for Multics by R. C. Daley and P. G. Neumann in 'A General-Purpose File System for Secondary Storage', presented at the AFIPS Fall Joint Computer Conference on 30 November to 1 December 1965. The paper cites no prior work for the idea, and no hierarchical file system is known to predate it.

source.title: Daley & Neumann, A General-Purpose File System for Secondary Storage, Proc. AFIPS 1965 FJCC vol. 27 pt. 1, pp. 213-229

claims.text: Daley was at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and Neumann at Bell Telephone Laboratories.

source.title: AFIPS '65 Fall Joint Computer Conference proceedings, author affiliations

claims.text: The paper states that anything not basic to a user's manipulation of information should remain invisible unless the user asks otherwise, and that information must be easy to access, safe from accident and malice, and shareable on a controllable basis.

source.title: Daley & Neumann, A General-Purpose File System for Secondary Storage, abstract

claims.text: Unix was written by Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie at Bell Labs; the first edition manual is dated 3 November 1971.

source.title: Thompson & Ritchie, UNIX Programmer's Manual, First Edition, 3 November 1971

claims.text: In Unix a directory is itself a file whose contents are pairs of a name and an i-number, and the i-number indexes the i-list, which holds the file's actual description. The name is therefore not a property of the file.

source.title: Ritchie & Thompson, The UNIX Time-Sharing System, CACM 17(7), July 1974

beats.broke: storage addressed by physical position; no namespace; two programs could target the same place with nothing to stop them
beats.fix: Multics 1965, Daley and Neumann: a directory is a file holding names and pointers, so names became a layer above physical position
beats.cost: a name is now an indirection: lookups walk a tree, a file can have several names or none, and deleting a name is not deleting data
beats.interview: why does deleting a file not erase it, and what does that tell you about what a folder holds
